source: Webb, Holyoak & Lu (2024) Evidence from counterfactual tasks supports emergent analogical reasoning in LLMs (reply to Hodel & West; Lewis & Mitchell)
finding: GPT-4 fails shuffled-alphabet letter-string analogies mainly because it cannot count letter positions. With code execution it solves them at human level, with no instruction to use code.
numbers: Humans N=99 (interval 1) and N=97 (interval 2). Interval-2 harder for humans P=1.5e-11 and GPT-4 P<2e-16; not significant for GPT-4+code P=0.066. Humans beat plain GPT-4 P=8.9e-13; GPT-4+code vs humans P=0.496. Model gpt-4-0125-preview.
quote: such problems require that letters be converted into the corresponding indices in the permuted alphabet, a process that depends on the ability to precisely count
limits: Same lab as the original claim. Bar heights are only in a figure; exact accuracies not in text. Code is not a human-like route. Only one counterfactual family (plus one more in S2.4).
agent_relevance: Gap 5 mostly closed: the counterfactual gap is a counting/indexing failure, not proof of no analogy. For our agent, give an external tool for position lookup before judging mapping skill.

source: Webb, Holyoak & Lu (2024) supplementary: error types and training-cutoff controls
finding: Controls against contamination: a new synthetic alphabet and an older GPT-4 engine (cutoff April 2023, before the Hodel & West problem set) gave the same results. GPT-4+code errors were often valid alternative rules, like human errors.
numbers: 46% (23/50) of GPT-4+code errors used a valid alternative rule vs 39% of human errors in Lewis & Mitchell. New vs old alphabet P=0.52; old vs new engine P=0.12 (logistic regression).
quote: Performance was driven almost entirely by the presence or absence of code execution.
limits: Non-significant P values do not prove equality; per-type counts are small. The 39% human rate is from another lab's sample.
agent_relevance: Supports using code/tool help for counting inside mapping tasks, and shows the agent's mistakes can be plausible alternative mappings, not noise.

source: Hodel & West (2023/2024) Response: Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: Argues Webb et al. 2023 is not truly zero-shot because letter-string problems circulate online, and that GPT-3 fails on simple variants (permuted alphabet) while humans stay high.
numbers: Text read this session gives the argument and a ChatGPT elicitation of letter-string examples. Numeric results are in the appendix figures and were not extractable.
quote: Without ruling out the possibility of data memorization, one cannot claim zero-shot reasoning.
limits: Exact accuracies not recorded. Webb et al. 2024 (d01) answer with code-execution and older-cutoff controls. Contamination cannot be fully excluded for older tasks.
agent_relevance: Use fresh, never-published mapping items when testing our agent; do not trust public analogy benchmarks as evidence of mapping skill.

source: Inani, Kabra, Marupudi & Varma (2025) Modeling understanding of story-based analogies using LLMs (CogSci 2025)
finding: Re-ran the 18 Gentner et al. 1993 story analogies on current models with answer order balanced (50 of 100 runs per item with the true analogy second). Larger and newer models reach or pass the human level; a self-generated-hints 2-step prompt raises accuracy.
numbers: Humans .847; GPT-3 (Webb) .75. Conventional prompt: gpt-4o-mini .7011, gpt-4o .8233, Llama-3.1-8B .6528, Llama-3.1-70B .8538. Enhanced prompt gives higher values for all four, best about .915 for 70B (column pairing of the enhanced numbers is inferred from a scrambled table). BERT embedding picks the true analogy on 78% of items. 100 runs per item, temperature 1.
quote: larger models perform at least 15% better than their smaller counterparts
limits: Only 18 items, so item-level noise is large. Enhanced-prompt column labels were scrambled in text extraction. No reasoning models tested. Humans are Webb's N=54 replication.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 partly closed: with order balanced, 2024 models are at human level on this small set; the order effect is controlled, not measured. A hint step before choosing is a cheap candidate for S4 mapping choice.

source: Inani et al. (2025) item-level human alignment
finding: Overall accuracy does not mean the same items are hard. Only the smallest conventional-prompt model tracked human item difficulty.
numbers: BERT similarity difference vs human item accuracy r=-0.032 (p=.899). gpt-4o-mini conventional r=.526 (p=.025), the only correlation different from 0. Enhanced prompting lowered correlation for 3 of 4 models (authors suspect ceiling). Models weak vs humans on items 3, 7, 13, 15, where both targets share entities and first-order relations.
limits: n=18 items; correlation CIs are wide. Ceiling effect confounds the enhanced-prompt result.
agent_relevance: A scaffold can raise accuracy while making errors less human-like; do not use human-likeness as the target, use correctness on fresh items.

source: Petersen, Stevenson & van der Plas (2025) Modelling analogies and analogical reasoning: connecting cognitive science theory and NLP research
finding: Survey restating Holyoak and Thagard: purpose should guide mapping (pragmatic centrality). It says getting a model to use the goal when choosing what to map is a hard open problem, especially for text with irrelevant content. No measured LLM test of goal-dependent mapping is cited.
quote: getting the model to consider the goal when making decisions could be challenging
limits: Review, not an experiment. Absence of citation is not proof that no test exists.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1 and 8 stay open: our own test (same ambiguous mapping under two goals) would be new evidence.

source: Spellman & Holyoak (1992) If Saddam is Hitler then who is George Bush? Analogical mapping between systems of social roles. JPSP 62, 913-933 - Experiment 1
finding: Survey of UCLA students on mapping the Gulf crisis to World War II (given Hussein = Hitler). Mappings for Bush and the US were interdependent: two coherent but incompatible patterns (bistable, like a Necker cube). Gap 9 closed with exact numbers.
numbers: 196 surveyed, 122 attempted mapping, 42 met criteria. Table 1: Bush=FDR with US-91=US-WW2 21; Bush=FDR with US-91=Britain 2; Bush=Churchill with US-WW2 6; Bush=Churchill with Britain 13. So 34/42 (81%) consistent; chi2(1,N=42)=16.16. Saudi Arabia: if US=US-WW2, 8 of 16 mapped it to Britain; if US=Britain, 0 of 7 did (chi2(1,N=23)=5.37). One-to-many among 122: Kuwait 12 subjects, US-91 9, Saudi 3, Iraq 3.
limits: Naturalistic survey, no control of knowledge; 80 of 122 excluded (mostly missing Bush or US mapping), so the 81% is for the retained subset. 1990s student sample.
agent_relevance: Good test set for our agent: Bush/US/Saudi triad where one-to-one pressure moves Saudi Arabia from Britain to France. Check whether the agent keeps leader and nation consistent.

source: Spellman & Holyoak (1992) Experiment 2: biased histories of World War II
finding: Four slanted histories (FDR-US, FDR-Britain, Churchill-US, Churchill-Britain) moved mappings, but only toward the consistent pairs. Histories pushing crossed pairs failed; people still produced consistent mappings.
numbers: 76 subjects, 50 usable. Overall effect chi2(9,N=50)=32.42. Consistent histories gave opposite patterns chi2(1,N=25)=11.65. Collapsing, 88% consistent (chi2(1,N=50)=26.60; Table 3: FDR-US 20, FDR-Britain 5, Churchill-US 1, Churchill-Britain 24); 89% under consistent histories vs 86% under crossed histories, chi2(1,N=50)=0.15 ns. Saudi Arabia shift chi2(1,N=26)=7.79. 26 of 76 dropped (13 failed, 13 one-to-many). Cells of 18-20 per condition.
limits: Small cells; 34% exclusion. The ACME simulations fit ordinally. Same lab as the theory.
agent_relevance: Shows a short slanted summary can steer a bistable mapping but cannot force an incoherent one: framing text in a scaffold works only inside consistent mapping options (supports K05).

source: Spellman & Holyoak (1992) Experiment 3: science-fiction countries, one-to-many mappings
finding: With plural wording ('matches'), one-to-many mapping rose in the crossed condition. Crossed condition produced one-to-many mappings, consistent condition none.
numbers: 67 UCLA students, 59 retained, 46 gave mappings. One-to-many mappings 41% in crossed vs 0% in consistent condition, chi2(1,N=46)=9.75, p<.01. 9 of 22 crossed subjects mapped the president/Anthar to the King.
limits: Other cell counts not extracted. Student sample. This is the 1992 precursor of the 1996 Anthar study (a09).
agent_relevance: One-to-one is a soft preference; the agent should allow a flagged one-to-many mapping when two source roles both fit the target.

source: Webb, Holyoak & Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in LLMs - digit-matrix relational complexity
finding: Relational load hurt both humans and GPT-3. More unique rules and progression (relation-defined) rules lowered accuracy; spatial permutation of corresponding elements lowered accuracy. Item-profile correlation human vs GPT-3 r(30)=0.39, p=.027.
numbers: Unique rules effect (3-rule problems): humans OR=0.61, p=.0047; GPT-3 OR=0.25, p=3e-10. Progression vs none: humans OR=0.41; GPT-3 OR=0.07. Spatial permutation: humans OR=0.52; GPT-3 OR=0.06. GPT-3 effects are steeper than human effects.
limits: This shows load effects but not the Krawczyk finding that surface similarity gains equal weight under load. No distractor-similarity manipulation. GPT-3 only.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 partly addressed: LLM accuracy falls with number of unique relations, steeper than for humans. Keep relations per mapping step low in the scaffold (split big mappings).

source: Webb, Holyoak & Lu (2023) story analogies and the Gick-Holyoak radiation problem with GPT-3
finding: Humans (N=54 UCLA undergraduates) beat GPT-3 on story analogies; GPT-3 was significant only for near analogies. GPT-4 pilot was stronger on far analogies. On the radiation problem, GPT-3 used the general story when it was presented alone, and with distractor stories only when told to consider earlier stories.
numbers: Combined: GPT-3 binomial p=0.0005; humans t(53)=21.3. Near: GPT-3 p=0.0039; far: GPT-3 p=0.065 (not significant), humans t(53)=16.7. GPT-3 vs humans OR=0.37, p=0.0003. 15/54 humans correct on every trial. Radiation problem: qualitative single runs.
limits: Single runs, qualitative for radiation. GPT-3 only; GPT-4 results are in the supplement.
agent_relevance: With distractor stories, spontaneous retrieval fails but an explicit 'check earlier material' prompt restores it; the scaffold's retrieval step should be an explicit instruction.

source: Musker, Duchnowski, Milliere & Pavlick (2025) LLMs as models for analogical reasoning, J. Memory and Language 145, 104676 - distractor conditions
finding: Semantic Structure task: with random (irrelevant) left-hand words, humans mostly ignore them but LLMs drop a lot. When the left side looks related, humans too are pulled by the random final word. Leakage of irrelevant structure is worse in models.
numbers: Only-RHS match to reference: GPT-4 about .9, Claude 3 and humans about .8, Llama-405B about .5 (GPT-4 vs humans p=.824). Humans drop about .15 in Randoms/Random Permuted Pairs; Claude 3 drops about .5, GPT-4 .6 and .4. All three models worse than humans in those conditions (GPT-4 coef -2.1972, z=-5.211, p<.001). Random Finals: humans fall about .5, GPT-4 by .8.
limits: Human sample size not extracted here. Models are 2024 era (gpt-4-0314, Claude 3 Opus, Llama-405B). Reasoning models not tested.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 partly closed (not for the goal, but for irrelevant structure): models are distracted by irrelevant items. Add an explicit step that drops items not needed for the goal.

source: Musker et al. (2025) follow-up: forcing use of left-right relations
finding: When the 2x2 task was widened so a right-hand-only shortcut fails, Claude 3 stayed at human level while GPT-4 and Llama-405B fell. Frontier models differ in mapping robustness.
numbers: Human and Claude 3 about .7 match; GPT-4 and Llama-405B about .35. GPT-4 vs humans coef -1.3669, z=-3.065, p=.002; Llama-405B coef -1.2550, p=.004; Claude 3 coef 0.2111, ns.
limits: Single follow-up condition; one run set per model. Could be prompt-sensitive (appendix shows prompt variation for GPT-4).
agent_relevance: Test our own base model for shortcut use (answering from the target side alone); do not assume another model's results transfer.

source: Musker et al. (2025) semantic content conditions: numeric and compositional
finding: GPT-4 matched or beat humans on Categorial and Dual-attribute mappings but fell to .2-.3 when mapping needed the number of characters (Numeric conditions). Claude 3 stayed at human level in all.
numbers: GPT-4 about .7 in Categorial and Dual-attribute (humans .7 and .4); GPT-4 better than humans in Dual-attribute (coef 1.0624, p=.015); worse in Numeric (coef -1.4781, p=.001) and Numeric Dual-attribute (coef -0.9694).
limits: Failure is tied to counting characters, parallel to the letter-string counting failure in d01.
agent_relevance: Counting/indexing is a recurring weak point; route it to a tool or an explicit enumeration step.

source: Lee, Song, Yoon, Park & Kang (2025/2026) The Curious Case of Analogies: investigating analogical reasoning in LLMs (AAAI 40)
finding: Inside open models, relation information is present in mid-upper layers in correct cases; failures often come from not applying the relation to the new entity. Story-analogy success goes with strong source-target structural alignment, and failures with distractor-biased alignment.
numbers: Patching fixed errors: overall +49.8% (Llama-2-13B), +61.9% (Gemma-7B), +55.3% (Qwen2.5-14B); Exp 1 +32.3/+38.4/+35.6; Exp 2 +25.9/+38.1/+30.5. Story samples 360 per model.
limits: Small open models only (13-14B), no reasoning models; patching is not usable at inference time by a prompt scaffold. Gains are relative to error sets defined by the authors.
agent_relevance: Supports splitting the step: (1) name the relation, (2) apply it to the new entity, since application, not encoding, is a bottleneck (gap 3 partial).

source: Colhoun & Gentner (2009) Inference processes in causal analogies (CogSci)
finding: Independent lab (structure-mapping camp) re-ran Lee & Holyoak causal-model inference studies and argued the effect inference can be judged after mapping, not only by a causal model. This tests an adjacent Holyoak-lab claim, not the 1996 goal-mapping result; no independent replication of the latter found.
numbers: Study 1A: effect-inference ratings GG 89.4, GGP 74.4, GP 46.1 (F(2,270)=164.6, p<.0001); similarity ratings GGP 7.53, GG 6.35, GP 5.01 (F(2,286)=44.4). An SME-based post-mapping calculation matched Lee & Holyoak data closely. About 70 Northwestern undergraduates in the Exp 1 replication (from search summary).
limits: Conference paper. Competing explanation, not a failure to reproduce the data pattern. Gap 10 stays open for mapping.
agent_relevance: Different camps agree on the data but not the mechanism: do not claim an ACME-specific mechanism in our design, only the behaviours.

source: Das & Balke (2025) From prototypical to relational: how LLMs navigate complex analogies (INLG 2025)
finding: Snippet only: on SAT-style analogies with several plausible answers, GPT-4 does well on embedding and prototypicality measures but underperforms on fine-grained relational mappings.
limits: Not opened; page and PDF not read this session.
agent_relevance: Another sign that multiple plausible mappings are a weakness; follow up before citing.

source: Are LLMs capable of deep relational reasoning? Insights from DeepSeek-R1 (arXiv 2506.23128)
finding: Snippet only: DeepSeek-R1 was best of three on family-tree and graph relational tasks, but all models degraded as problem size grew and R1's long chains were sometimes incoherent. Not an analogy-mapping test.
limits: Not opened; adjacent task, not analogy. Authors not verified.
agent_relevance: Only a hint that reasoning models still lose at larger relational load; gap 3 for reasoning models stays open.
